bill.title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to "California State Motor Vehicle and Engine Pollution Control Standards; Advanced Clean Cars II; Waiver of Preemption; Notice of Decision".
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
subjects: Hybrid, electric, and advanced technology vehicles

industries.rationale: Automotive manufacturers would face different regulatory obligations depending on whether California's distinct emission standards remain in effect.
The Advanced Clean Cars II regulations affect the market for electric vehicle charging infrastructure and clean-energy vehicle adoption.
Electric utilities face demand changes tied to electric vehicle adoption rates influenced by state emission standards.
Petroleum refiners and distributors face market impacts from regulations that affect the mix of gasoline versus electric vehicles sold.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would overturn an Environmental Protection Agency decision that allowed California to enforce its Advanced Clean Cars II regulations. Those regulations set emission standards for vehicles sold in California that differ from federal standards. If passed, the resolution would nullify the waiver that permits California to apply its own rules.

bill.title: TAKE IT DOWN Act
bill.latestActionText: Became Public Law No: 119-12.

industries.rationale: The bill directly imposes new content moderation obligations and 48-hour removal requirements on social media platforms and user-generated content websites.
New criminal prohibitions and mandatory restitution provisions would generate litigation and enforcement work related to intimate image publication.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would make it a federal crime to publish intimate images or videos of someone online without their consent, including computer-generated deepfakes, when the publication is intended to cause harm or involves a minor. Social media platforms and similar websites would be required to remove such content within 48 hours after receiving a complaint from the person depicted. Violators would face criminal penalties including prison time, fines, and mandatory restitution to victims.

plain.whoItTouches: Children, and the adults responsible for them. Anyone who uses the internet.

bill.latestActionText: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 495.

The bill aims to integrate grazing into broader wildfire prevention and forest management strategies on public lands.

bill.title: BANNED in Latin America Act
bill.latestActionText: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 514.

industries.rationale: The bill ties foreign assistance to ICC investigations of U.S. nationals, which could affect defense cooperation and security assistance programs in the region.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would prohibit U.S. foreign assistance to countries in Latin America and the Caribbean that have diplomatic or economic relations with the International Criminal Court if the Court is investigating or prosecuting U.S. or Israeli nationals. The prohibition would apply unless the President certifies that the country has severed such relations or determines that providing aid is in the national security interest of the United States.

bill.title: Rural Broadband Protection Act of 2025
bill.latestActionText: Became Public Law No: 119-89.

industries.rationale: The bill directly regulates eligibility and vetting for broadband providers seeking federal subsidies to deploy networks in rural areas.
Some internet service providers and broadband infrastructure companies in the technology sector may apply for these rural deployment funds.

bill.plainSummary: This bill directs the Federal Communications Commission to create a formal screening process for companies applying for federal funding to build broadband networks in rural and other high-cost areas. Applicants would need to prove they have the technical skills, financial resources, and realistic business plans to complete the projects, and the FCC would check their track record with other government broadband programs. Companies that fail to meet these standards after applying would face financial penalties, and only those who pass the vetting would receive funding.

bill.title: Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Reauthorization Act of 2026
bill.latestActionText: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 461.
subjects: Department of Health and Human Services

industries.rationale: The bill directly funds research and development of drugs and therapies for ALS and neurodegenerative diseases, affecting pharmaceutical and biotech companies developing these treatments.
Clinical trial enrollment requirements and expanded access to investigational drugs may affect hospitals and health systems conducting ALS research and treatment.

bill.plainSummary: This bill extends funding through fiscal year 2031 for federal programs that support research and development of treatments for ALS (Lou Gehrig's disease) and similar neurodegenerative diseases. It requires the National Institutes of Health to track safety data more closely when awarding grants for experimental drug studies, and directs the Food and Drug Administration to publish five-year plans describing how it will help develop and approve treatments for these rare diseases. The bill also mandates reports evaluating the effectiveness of these grant programs.

bill.title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to "Review of Final Rule Reclassification of Major Sources as Area Sources Under Section 112 of the Clean Air Act".
bill.latestActionText: Became Public Law No: 119-20.

industries.rationale: Industrial manufacturers are frequently classified as major sources of hazardous air pollutants and would face changed regulatory obligations regarding emission controls after reclassification.
Fossil fuel facilities often emit hazardous air pollutants and would be directly affected by changes to emission control requirements when reclassifying source status.
Mining and materials processing operations can be major sources of hazardous air pollutants subject to these reclassification rules.
Waste management facilities may emit hazardous air pollutants and could be affected by changes to emission control requirements during source reclassification.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would nullify an EPA rule that requires industrial facilities to maintain strict emission controls when they reduce their pollution output enough to reclassify from "major source" to "area source" status under the Clean Air Act. The EPA rule was designed to prevent facilities from increasing emissions of persistent and bioaccumulative hazardous air pollutants after reclassifying to the less stringent area source category. If this resolution passes, facilities that reclassify would no longer be required to continue using the emission control methods that were mandatory when they were classified as major sources.

plain.whoItTouches: People living near a road, a plant or a port.

bill.title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Federal Communications Commission relating to "Addressing the Homework Gap Through the E-Rate Program".
bill.latestActionText: Held at the desk.

industries.rationale: The bill would eliminate a new revenue stream for wireless carriers and broadband providers who sell hotspots and mobile connectivity services to schools and libraries under the E-Rate program.
The bill would remove schools' and libraries' ability to purchase subsidized internet access equipment for students and patrons, affecting their budgets and service delivery.
The bill would affect manufacturers and vendors of Wi-Fi hotspot devices that would have been purchased through the expanded E-Rate program.

bill.plainSummary: This resolution would overturn a Federal Communications Commission rule that allows schools and libraries to use E-Rate program funds to purchase Wi-Fi hotspots and mobile internet service for students and patrons to use at home. The FCC rule was designed to help students complete homework and access educational resources outside of school buildings. If this resolution passes, that rule would be nullified and schools and libraries would no longer be able to use E-Rate funds for off-campus internet access.

bill.title: Protecting Access for Hunters and Anglers Act of 2025
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.

industries.rationale: The bill directly affects manufacturers and sellers of lead ammunition by limiting federal authority to regulate their products on public lands.
Manufacturers of fishing tackle containing lead would face fewer potential federal restrictions on their products' use.
Sporting goods retailers selling lead ammunition and tackle would benefit from reduced regulatory uncertainty around these product lines.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would prevent three federal agencies—the Fish and Wildlife Service, Bureau of Land Management, and Forest Service—from banning or regulating the use of lead ammunition or fishing tackle on federal lands and waters. The agencies could still impose restrictions in specific locations if they determine, based on field data from that site, that lead use is the primary cause of a wildlife population decline and the state agrees to the regulation. Certain existing regulations would remain in place.

bill.title: Laken Riley Act
bill.latestActionText: Became Public Law No: 119-1.

industries.rationale: The bill directly imposes new detention mandates on DHS and creates liability exposure for federal agencies, while authorizing state governments to bring suit over immigration enforcement.

The bill creates new grounds for state litigation against the federal government and expands detention requirements, generating demand for legal services in immigration and intergovernmental litigation.

bill.plainSummary: This bill requires the Department of Homeland Security to detain certain non-citizens who are in the country unlawfully and have been arrested for or charged with crimes including burglary, theft, assault on law enforcement, or offenses causing death or serious injury. It also allows state governments to sue the federal government if immigration enforcement decisions or failures—such as releasing detainees, not conducting required asylum interviews, or violating parole limitations—cause harm to the state or its residents, including financial harm exceeding $100.

bill.title: Fair Access to Banking Act
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.

industries.rationale: The bill directly regulates how banks and credit unions may deny financial services to customers.
Digital asset firms have frequently reported being denied banking services, making them likely beneficiaries of fair-access requirements.
Firearms businesses have reported service denials from banks citing reputational risk, which this bill would prohibit.
Cannabis and related businesses have faced banking access challenges that this bill's requirements could address.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would restrict banks, credit unions, and payment card networks from refusing service to customers who comply with the law. Financial institutions could only deny service based on documented, quantitative risk standards set in advance, and could not cite reputational concerns as a reason. Violations would trigger penalties including loss of federal deposit insurance, exclusion from electronic payment systems, and potential civil lawsuits by affected customers.

bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

industries.rationale: The bill directly deregulates silencers, reducing compliance costs and expanding the legal market for manufacturers and dealers of these products.

districtAwards.description: THE BEAD PROGRAM PROVIDES FEDERAL FUNDING FOR GRANTS TO ELIGIBLE ENTITIES FOR BROADBAND PLANNING, DEPLOYMENT, MAPPING, EQUITY, AND ADOPTION ACTIVITIES. THE PROGRAM'S PRINCIPAL FOCUS WILL BE ON DEPLOYING BROADBAND SERVICE TO UNSERVED LOCATIONS AND UNDERSERVED LOCATIONS. ELIGIBLE ENTITIES THAT DEMONSTRATE THEY WILL BE ABLE TO ENSURE SERVICE TO ALL UNSERVED AND UNDERSERVED LOCATIONS WILL BE FREE TO PROPOSE PLANS THAT USE REMAINING FUNDS IN A WIDE VARIETY OF WAYS, BUT NTIA UNDERSCORES ITS STRONG PREFERENCE THAT ELIGIBLE ENTITIES ALSO ENSURE DEPLOYMENT OF GIGABIT CONNECTIONS TO COMMUNITY ANCHOR INSTITUTIONS SUCH AS LIBRARIES AND COMMUNITY CENTERS THAT LACK SUCH CONNECTIVITY. ELIGIBLE ENTITIES CAN APPLY ANY ADDITIONAL FUNDING TO PURSUE ELIGIBLE ACCESS-, ADOPTION-, AND EQUITY-RELATED USES, AS WELL AS ANY OTHER USES APPROVED BY THE ASSISTANT SECRETARY THAT SUPPORT THE PROGRAM'S GOALS.THE PROPOSED PROJECT INCLUDES THE FOLLOWING ACTIVITIES TO BE PERFORMED, DELIVERABLES, AND EXPECTED OUTCOMES: FUNDS TO BE USED FOR INITIAL PLANNING AND PRE-DEPLOYMENT ACTIVITIES; FUNDS TO BE USED, DIRECTLY OR INDIRECTLY, FOR THE ADMINISTRATION OF THE GRANT; FUNDS TO BE USED FOR ADMINISTRATIVE PURPOSES, OTHER THAN FOR THE ADMINISTRATION OF THE GRANT; FUNDS TO BE USED FOR PROGRAMMATIC USE (CHALLENGE & SUBGRANTEE PROCESS AND EXECUTION); AND FUNDS TO BE USED UPON NTIA APPROVAL OF THE FINAL PROPOSAL.THE INTENDED BENEFICIARIES ARE THE UTAH BROADBAND CENTER AND PRINCIPALLY UNSERVED AND UNDERSERVED COMMUNITIES IN UTAH. THE RECIPIENT DOES INTEND TO SUBAWARD FUNDS.
